posts.title: How to Scale and Accelerate Distributed Digital Ising Machines
posts.subtitle: A calibrated performance model and a systematic framework for system-level acceleration
posts.author: Tong Wu et al. · CMU · Pitt · UCSB
posts.tldr: Large Ising problems outgrow one device and expose three system costs: coupling data moving through the memory hierarchy, colored Gibbs updates synchronising, and boundary states crossing device links. We separate these costs in a performance model calibrated across GPUs, FPGAs, and ASICs. Roofline analysis shows Ising workloads have low arithmetic intensity, and measurements show performance drops sharply once the working set spills beyond on-chip storage. We develop two systematic approaches to system-level acceleration: bounded-staleness sampling reduces synchronisation frequency, and a phase-offset pipeline places boundary exchange behind interior computation. A fabricated multi-chip ASIC implements the streaming schedule.

posts.title: Scaling changes the problem
posts.tldr: Practical problems outgrow one accelerator's on-chip storage, so the coupling graph must be partitioned across devices — creating a memory boundary inside each device and a communication boundary between them. The right question is not which device is fastest, but which term limits this workload at this size and mapping.

posts.title: One equation locates the bottleneck
posts.tldr: A four-term model — compute, memory, synchronisation, communication — locates the limiting factor in each sweep, and holds for dynamically scheduled GPUs as well as statically scheduled FPGAs and ASICs. A single calibration per GPU predicts performance at block sizes withheld from calibration, because each parameter represents a physical mechanism rather than a fitted curve.

posts.title: Roofline analysis exposes low arithmetic intensity
posts.tldr: The first roofline analysis of Ising workloads shows their arithmetic intensity stays low even as graph degree rises, because operations and bytes grow together. On-chip residency marks the main crossover: once the coupling working set spills, sweep time rises sharply. Coupling precision and sparse format (CSR vs. ELLPACK) decide where that crossover lands.

posts.title: Two forms of bounded-staleness sampling
posts.tldr: Multi-rate bounded staleness postpones boundary-state propagation to interior p-bits; cross-partition bounded staleness postpones propagation across a partition boundary. Both bound the age of an observed neighbour state with the same parameter F. Measurements show an interior optimum in time-to-solution — past it, quality loss dominates and time-to-solution rises again.

posts.title: Phase-offset pipelining hides boundary exchange
posts.tldr: A device updates its boundary early, dispatches the packet immediately, then computes interior spins while it travels. A link becomes latency-transparent when the whole transfer fits inside that gap — bytes still cross, but communication stops contributing to sweep time. Bandwidth alone cannot guarantee this: the device also needs enough interior work to cover link latency.

posts.title: A fabricated four-chip system
posts.tldr: A chain of fabricated ASICs implements the streaming design, with local SRAM holding one Pegasus-graph partition per chip. Across the tested chip counts each added chip raises aggregate throughput without increasing cycles per sweep. Partitioning can beat ordinary parallel speedup — because the working set moves from off-chip memory into on-chip storage, not from superlinear compute scaling.

posts.title: Five checks that guide system design
posts.tldr: Test residency first; treat synchronisation as a quality parameter and report time-to-solution; size the device and link together; match partition geometry to the graph; and compare schedules at equal solution quality. The best distributed Ising accelerator is not the one with the fastest spin update — it is the one that keeps data resident and makes coordination invisible at the target graph size.

posts.title: What the result does not claim
posts.tldr: The experiments target sparse hardware graphs — kings and Pegasus topologies. Dense all-to-all instances occupy a different regime and scale poorly on distributed digital hardware. Neither staleness mechanism preserves exact Gibbs sampling: both trade a measured amount of solution quality for throughput.
